meta.tagline: The White Isle: turquoise coves, hippie markets and sunset rituals

pills: The White Isle — La Isla Blanca
Two-faced: from superclubs to silent coves

overview.title: Welcome to Ibiza
overview.intro: Ibiza's fame was written by its nightclubs, but the island's real story is older: the Phoenicians built a port, ramparts rose against pirates, the hippies of the sixties settled the pine-fringed coves — and all of them left their mark on this white island. Today history lives in Dalt Vila's stone lanes, silence in the northern coves, a sunset rite opposite Es Vedrà, and at night the world's most famous dancefloors. There are two Ibizas — in what dose you mix them is entirely up to you.

local_word.definition: The island's Catalan and official name: the road signs say 'Eivissa', not 'Ibiza'. A local introduces themselves as 'eivissenc' — using this name shows you entered the island through its door, not its brochure.

rules.title: Get to know both islands
rules.description: South means night, north means silence: San Antonio and Playa d'en Bossa are party, the north around Portinatx and Benirràs is pine and cove. Whoever settles for one face has missed half the island.

rules.title: Never buy the club ticket at the door
rules.description: The big clubs' door prices are punishing: tickets are clearly cheaper online and in advance sales, and most hotels and bars pre-sell. As for the dream of two clubs in one night — that's budget and energy suicide.

rules.title: Coves early, sunset in position
rules.description: The famous calas fill by noon and the car parks overflow: 10 am is a cove's finest hour. For sunset it's the place, not the time, that matters — the cliffs opposite Es Vedrà or the west coast rocks need a plan.

quick_facts.sub: 10 min to town · direct flights in season

quick_facts.label: On the island
quick_facts.sub: Buses on main lines, weak to the coves

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: English everywhere on the tourist trail

tip.label: The Ibiza philosophy
tip.text: The island's local rhythm is 'poc a poc' — little by little: a cove in the morning, a long table at noon, sunset in the evening, the dancefloor at night if you wish. Whoever crams it all into one day lives none of it.

transport.title: Getting Around the Island
transport.intro: Ibiza looks small but its coves are scattered: freedom is a rental car, practicality the main bus lines, pleasure a boat.

items.title: Airport to town
items.description: The airport is 10 minutes from Ibiza Town: bus 10 runs frequently in season, and taxis stay near a flat rate. Crossing to the San Antonio side takes half an hour.

items.title: A rental car — the key to the coves
items.description: Most hidden coves are reached down dirt tracks; a small car is the island's key. Book early in summer and reach beach car parks in the morning — by noon a space is down to luck.

items.title: The main bus lines
items.description: The Ibiza-San Antonio-Santa Eulària triangle and the airport line run regularly; at night the Disco Bus links the clubs. Services to the northern coves are sparse — check times beforehand.

items.title: Boats and ferries
items.description: The Formentera ferry leaves the port every half hour; coastal boats work like taxis on the Cala Comte-Cala Bassa line. The sunset cruise past Es Vedrà is the island's classic gesture.

items.title: Scooters and bikes
items.description: A scooter is practical for short hops and the harbour area; the inland roads are hilly and hot in summer — the bicycle is an early-morning vehicle.

callout.label: Formentera tip
callout.text: Cross to Formentera on the first ferry, rent a bike at the quay and slip into Ses Illetes' Caribbean water before the crowds: sunburn and the regret of 'why didn't we stay a night' are standard on the ferry back.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Ibiza the choice of area decides the kind of holiday: harbour and rampart shade, party beach, family cove or the pine silence of the north.

local_word.definition: Country hotels converted from old farmhouses in the island's interior: stone walls, fig trees, poolside breakfasts. Ibiza's 'other face' is best lived in these white fincas.

items.name: Ibiza Town (Eivissa) and Dalt Vila
items.description: Stone lanes inside the walls, the evening paseo along the harbour, marina bars: the centre of the history + nightlife balance. Lively and expensive in summer — the showcase of island life.

items.name: Santa Eulària des Riu
items.description: A calm promenade, sandy beaches and restaurant variety: far from the party, firmly on comfort's side. The classic base for families and quiet holidaymakers.

items.name: San Antonio (Sant Antoni)
items.description: The shore of the Sunset Strip and the young party crowd: the sunset bars are legend, night noise guaranteed. With budget hotels and the boat-trip harbour, the address of youth.

items.name: The north — Portinatx and Sant Joan
items.description: Pine forests, hidden coves and villages with a hippie inheritance: the island's slow face. A car is essential; the reward is silence and a starry sky.

items.name: Inland — Santa Gertrudis and the fincas
items.description: White village squares and agroturismo fincas: equal distance to every cove, long tables on the village square at night. For those who want Ibiza as an island village.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Read Ibiza's calendar not by the club season but by light and crowds: June and September are gold, July-August the peak, winter another island entirely.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Opening Season
items.subtitle: Spring · A green island, opening parties
items.description: The island turns its liveliest green with wildflowers, the sea becomes swimmable in May, and late May-June opens the season's gate with the clubs' opening parties. The coves are calm, prices still reasonable.

callout.label: June tip
callout.text: The first half of June is the island's equilibrium: the sea warmed, the opening parties done, the August crowds far away. This is the window where the cove + club mix comes together most easily.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Peak Season
items.subtitle: Summer · Full coves, world-class nights
items.description: The world's DJ calendar moves to the island, the coves and roads fill, prices hit the ceiling. The energy is unmatched, but nobody should come unplanned: club ticket, restaurant table and car — all three in advance.

callout.label: August note
callout.text: Arriving at the famous calas at noon in August is a disappointment: go between 9 and 10 am or approach by boat. Don't trust the taxi queue — plan the night's return by Disco Bus or a pre-arranged transfer.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Closings and a Warm Sea
items.subtitle: Autumn · September balance, closing parties
items.description: September is the island's best secret: the sea at its warmest, the crowds receded, and in early October the closing parties play the finale. With November the island returns to its locals and the hiking season opens.

callout.label: September tip
callout.text: Come in late September: summer sea in empty coves by day, the 'last dance' energy of the closing parties by night. The same hotel costs half its August price — the island's two smartest weeks.

items.label: Winter
items.name: The Locals' Island
items.subtitle: Winter · Almond blossom, empty trails
items.description: The clubs sleep and the island breathes: in January and February the almond trees turn white, and the coastal paths belong to walkers. Many places close, but Dalt Vila and the village markets live on in their true form.

callout.label: February tip
callout.text: Catch the almond blossom of the Santa Agnès plain in February: a sea of white flowers, red earth behind, and silence — the Ibiza postcard nobody knows.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The island's cooking comes out of fishermen's pots: saffron fish stews, village-style meats and century-old liqueur recipes — the real Ibiza behind the beach club menus.

local_word.definition: The island's signature dish: the day's fish poached in saffron-garlic broth, the fish served first, then arroz a banda rice cooked in that same broth. One order, two magnificent plates — the classic of the fishing coves.

items.name: Bullit de peix — fish in two acts
items.description: First the saffron-poached fish and potatoes, then in act two the rice of that same broth, arroz a banda: the island's greatest gastronomic pride. In family restaurants of the fishing coves — with a booking if possible.
items.tag: At a fishing-cove restaurant · two servings

items.name: Sofrit pagès — the village pot
items.description: The village classic where chicken, lamb, sausage and potatoes meet over slow fire: the heart of the winter table, on menus in summer too. Filling and honest — the signature of the agroturismo kitchens.

items.name: Flaó and greixonera
items.description: Flaó: the fresh-cheese-and-mint tart, Ibiza's unchanged dessert of centuries. Greixonera is a cinnamon pudding made from yesterday's ensaimada — a masterpiece of the island's waste-nothing mind.
items.tag: The dessert duo · the minted flaó is a must

items.name: Hierbas ibicencas
items.description: The anise liqueur steeped with dozens of island herbs — pine, fennel and mint among them: served over ice after dinner. Every family has its bottle and every restaurant its recipe — a classic gift, too.

items.name: Ensalada payesa and peix sec
items.description: The village salad, Ibiza-style: potatoes, red peppers and sun-dried fish (peix sec). Salty, fresh, the lightest victory of a beach noon.

items.name: The chiringuito sunset table
items.description: Grilled fish, sangria and feet in the sand at the beach bars: a simple menu, a magnificent stage. At the west coast chiringuitos, claim the table an hour before sunset.
items.tag: On the west coast · before sunset

callout.label: The booking rule
callout.text: In summer a good fish restaurant is harder to get than a beach club: bullit de peix needs pre-ordering in most places. The 'authentic Ibiza' you're after is not at the beach club but in the family pot at the cove's end — call a day ahead.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone knows the famous coves; these six are the island's concealed face.

items.name: The Es Vedrà lookouts
items.description: The uninhabited rock rising 380 metres from the sea is the centre of all the island's legends: sirens, magnetic fields, the home of Tanit. Watch at sunset from the cliffs above Cala d'Hort or the Savinar tower — the crowd on the beach, you up above.

items.name: Benirràs
items.description: The north's pine-belted cove sees the sun off with a drum circle on Sunday evenings: the place where the hippie legacy still breathes. Go early — the cove is small, the ritual famous.

items.rarity: An island market within the island
items.name: Las Dalias and the hippie markets
items.description: The legendary market at Sant Carles has been set up since 1954: handmade jewellery, the island's last true hippies and live music. Saturday is the main day — go in the morning, leave before the midday crowd.

items.name: The Ses Salines salt pans
items.description: The salt pools worked since the Phoenicians turn pink at sunset; flamingos wade the shallows. The beach's fame overshadows the pans' quiet beauty — tour them by bicycle.

items.name: Torre des Savinar (Torre del Pirata)
items.description: The 18th-century watchtower directly opposite Es Vedrà: a short, steep path leads up, and the reward is the island's most dramatic view. Be at the top an hour before sunset.

items.name: A Santa Gertrudis evening
items.description: The white village of the interior: tapas bars, galleries and tables under the trees around the square. An evening's break from the coastal noise — village Ibiza with a plate of jamón and a cold white.

callout.label: Cove tip
callout.text: Every cove written large on the map has a 'little neighbour': if Cala Comte is full walk to Cala Escondida, if Cala Bassa overflows walk to Cala Gracioneta. A five-minute path means half the crowd.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: In summer Ibiza can be one of the world's most expensive islands per tourist; these four are the budget's main insurance.

items.name: Buying the club ticket at the door
items.description: The door price sits well above the advance sale; inside, even water is serious money, and the 'free entry' flyers usually hide a drinks condition.
items.instead: Buy the ticket early from official sales and plan one club per night. Enter knowing the drinks budget — an island night's true cost is the ticket plus three drinks.

items.name: The beach club sunbed's small print
items.description: The front-row beds' minimum spend reaches the price of a full lunch; once seated, there is no bargaining.
items.instead: Ask the minimum spend before sitting, or live the same sea for free on a towel on the public side. Choose a beach club as a deliberate experience, not a default.

items.name: Expecting a taxi on an August night
items.description: Island taxis are few, and in peak season the night queues pass an hour; the 'we'll just grab a taxi' plan collapses at club exit.
items.instead: Learn the Disco Bus lines, arrange the return in advance or book a group transfer. If you rented a car, appoint the night's driver from the start.

items.name: The 'all-inclusive' boat party
items.description: The cheap-looking boat parties run on a formula of crowded decks, restricted drinks and short anchor drops far from the good coves.
items.instead: Split a small-group sunset cruise or a private charter: let the route pass Es Vedrà and the stop be a real cove. Compare the price per boat, not per head.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Ibiza the most expensive thing is the lack of a plan: ticket, table, car and transfer — all four cost half to those who book early. And the island's finest things are still free: the cove, the path, the sunset and the sound of drums.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the walls to the cove, from the cove to the sunset rite

steps.title: A Dalt Vila morning
steps.description: Enter through the rampart gate and climb the stone lanes to the cathedral terrace: the harbour and Formentera at your feet, the crowds still asleep.

steps.title: The sea at the western coves
steps.description: Into Cala Comte's turquoise or its small neighbour: the best hours are before the midday crowd. Don't forget the snorkel.

steps.title: A chiringuito lunch
steps.description: Ensalada payesa + grilled fish with feet in the sand; minted flaó for dessert. A long shaded break after — the island rhythm demands it.

steps.title: The pink hour at Ses Salines
steps.description: A walk or bike ride through the salt flats: flamingos, salt hills and the lowering light. A short swim at its beach as a bonus.

steps.title: The Es Vedrà sunset rite
steps.description: Climb the Savinar tower path or settle on the cliffs above Cala d'Hort: the rock turns first to gold, then to ember. The silence arrives on its own.

steps.title: Night: village or dancefloor
steps.description: For a calm finale, tapas on the Santa Gertrudis square; for the grand one, a club night on a pre-bought ticket — both are legitimate Ibiza.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: The island's three faces: history, coves, soul

steps.title: Classic Ibiza
steps.description: The one-day flow above: Dalt Vila, the western coves, the salt pans, Es Vedrà.

steps.title: The Formentera escape
steps.description: Cross on the first ferry and rent a bike: Ses Illetes' Caribbean water, the inland paths and the lighthouse road. Ice cream + sunset at a harbour bar on the return.

steps.title: The soul of the north
steps.description: The Las Dalias market in the morning (if it's Saturday) or the village of Sant Joan; a swim in the northern coves at noon; the drummed sunset at Benirràs in the evening — this is how you say goodbye to the island.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Spanish opens every door on the island, and a pinch of Catalan guarantees a smile.

items.meaning: Hello / good morning — Catalan 'bon dia' is a gesture to the locals
Thank you — keep it ready in both languages
Please — valid when asking the sunbed price too
Cheers! — as the hierbas glass rises
'Little by little, take it easy' — the island's tempo; smile when you hear it, then apply it
